rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil says mention of al-Rahman drove them farther from faith.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: يقول (¬1): زادهم ذكر الرحمن تباعدا من الإيمان

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the Prophet's command to prostrate increased their aversion to what they were ordered to do.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: زادهم أمر النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- إياهم بالسجود نفورا

rows.speaker: عبد الأعلى
rows.claim: Mas'ar reports that Abd al-A'la prayed in prostration that God increase the worshippers' humility as enemies grow more averse, and not cast their faces into Hell after they prostrate.
rows.anchor: روى مسعر، عن عبد الأعلى (¬4)، أنه كان يقول في سجوده: زادنا لك خشوعا

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth defines hawn as the verbal noun of hayyin, meaning calmness and dignity.
rows.anchor: قال الليث (¬5): الهون: مصدر الهين في معنى (¬6) السكينة والوقار

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A saying attributed to Ali advises loving a beloved with moderation.
rows.anchor: وجاء عن علي رضي الله عنه: (أحبب حبيبك هونا ما)

rows.speaker: شمر
rows.claim: Shammar glosses hawn as gentleness, ease, and moderation, advising against excess in love or hatred; the cited hemistich uses hawn for gentle movement.
rows.anchor: قال شمر في تفسيره: الهون: الرفق، والدعة، والهينة، يقول: لا تفرط في حبه ولا بغضه

rows.speaker: شمر
rows.claim: Shammar cites a poetic line in which hawn describes gliding gently in a cloak; the poet is unnamed.
rows.anchor: وأنشد: تهادى في رداء المرط هونا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets walking humbly as walking with calmness and dignity; Mujahid gives the same gloss.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد بالسكينة والوقار (¬3). وهو لفظ مجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن، وعطاء، والضحاك، ومقاتل
rows.claim: Hasan, Ata, al-Dahhak, and Maqatil describe them as forbearing and humble, walking at a measured pace.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن، وعطاء، والضحاك، ومقاتل: حلماء متواضعين، يمشون في اقتصاد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains their measured walk as humility before God because of His greatness.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: {يمشون على الأرض هونا} تواضعا لله لعظمته

rows.speaker: أسامة بن زيد عن أبيه
rows.claim: A report from Usama ibn Zayd, from his father, says they do not stride forcefully.
rows.anchor: وروى أسامة بن زيد، عن أبيه، قال: لا يشتدون

rows.speaker: ابن وهب
rows.claim: Ibn Wahb says they neither act arrogantly toward people nor behave tyrannically.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن وهب: لا يتكبرون على الناس، ولا يتجبرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hawn is accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun: they walk a humble, measured walk.
rows.anchor: وانتصب {هونا}؛ لأنه صفة مصدر محذوف، أي: يمشون مشيا # هونا

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators treat this as a quality of God's chosen servants, whom He associates with Himself as in expressions such as God's House and God's she-camel.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: هذا من صفة خواص عباد الله، أضافهم إليه لاصطفائه إياهم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil glosses the ignorant interlocutors as fools and says the servants answered harm from Meccan unbelievers courteously.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: يعني السفهاء (¬3) {قالوا سلاما} يقول: إذا سمعوا الأذى من كفار مكة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the verse was abrogated by the fighting verse.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: نسختها آية القتال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets their answer as sound speech, so they do not answer ignorance with ignorance; Mujahid gives the same interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: ردوا سدادا من القول (¬6)، لا يجهلون مع من يجهل. وهذا قول مجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says that when an ignorant person wrongs them, they show forbearance rather than responding ignorantly.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: إن جهل عليهم جاهل حلموا ولم يجهلوا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says they did not behave ignorantly toward the people of the pre-Islamic age.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة. كانوا لا يجاهلون أهل الجاهلية

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: Maqatil ibn Hayyan glosses salām as speech by which they remain free of sin.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل بن حيان: {قالوا سلما} أي: قولا يسلمون فيه من الإثم

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق، وأبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq and Abu Ali understand the response as a peaceful greeting and withdrawal: they will not answer the ignorant in kind or become entangled in their conduct.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق، وأبو علي: نتسلم منكم سلاما لا نجاهلكم كأنهم قالوا

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abu al-Haytham defines it as sound, purposeful speech without frivolity, matching Ibn Hayyan's sense.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الهيثم: معناه: سدادا من القول، وقصدا لا لغو فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi rejects abrogation: this describes God's elite servants, who do not respond ignorantly or obscenely but show forbearance.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن لا تكون هذه الآية منسوخة؛ لأنها صفة لخواص من عباد الله

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq parses ʿibād as a nominative subject; its best predicate is the sentence at the end of the sura, though “those who walk” can also be the predicate and the next description can modify it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: {وعباد} مرفوع بالابتداء، والأحسن أن يكون الخبر: ما جاء في آخر السورة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says the walking describes their daytime among people, while their private night with their Lord is devoted to worship and prayer.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: هذا صفة نهارهم إذا انتشروا في الناس، وليلهم (¬3) خير ليل إذا خلو فيما بينهم وبين ربهم يراوحون بين أطرافهم

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة، والأخفش، والمبرد، وجميع النحويين
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda, al-Akhfash, al-Mubarrad, and the grammarians take rasūl here to mean risāla, “message”; the verse then means “we are bearers of a message from the Lord of the worlds,” with the head noun omitted.
rows.anchor: مذهب أبي عبيدة، والأخفش، والمبرد، وجميع النحويين: أن الرسول هاهنا بمعنى الرسالة

rows.speaker: كثير
rows.claim: The poet Kathir's line uses rasūl to mean a message, supporting the grammatical interpretation.
rows.anchor: لقد كذب الواشون ما بحت عندهم ... بسر ولا أرسلتهم برسول

rows.speaker: عباس بن مرداس
rows.claim: Abbas ibn Mirdas also uses rasūl for a message; the feminine agreement in the line supports that sense.
rows.anchor: وقول عباس بن مرداس: ألا من مبلغ عني خفافا ... رسولا بيت أهلك منتهاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the message reading, the construction means “we are possessors of a message from the Lord of the worlds,” with a genitive noun omitted.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا تقدير الآية: إنا ذو رسالة رب العالمين فحذف المضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another grammatical view takes the singular rasūl collectively, as in singular collective uses of enemy and friend; the cited Hudhali line uses rasūl for a group of informants.
rows.anchor: وفيه قول آخر؛ وهو: أن الرسول هاهنا في معنى جمع

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali gives both parses: rasūl may mean the sent person or the message; here he takes it as message with an omitted “possessors of,” while allowing a singular to stand for a dual or plural.
rows.anchor: وذكر أبو علي القولين جميعا بعبارة وجيزة، فقال: الرسول يستعمل على ضربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative omits that Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and delivered the message before Pharaoh's reply.
rows.anchor: في الكلام محذوف تقديره: فأتياه وأبلغا الرسالة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil says Pharaoh recognized Moses because he had raised him in his own house.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: عرف فرعون موسى؛ لأنه رباه في بيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walīd here means a young child or newborn; Moses was born among them and remained there until adulthood.
rows.anchor: والوليد: هو المولود، وموسى ولد فيهم ثم كان فيما بينهم حتى صار رجلا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses walīd as a small child and says Moses stayed with them for eighteen years.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: صغيرا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas estimates Moses' years among them at eighteen.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد ثمان عشرة سنة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil estimates Moses' years among them at thirty.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: ثلاثين سنة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi estimates Moses' years among them at forty.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: أربعين سنة

rows.speaker: مجاهد، ومقاتل، وقتادة، والسدي
rows.claim: Mujahid, Maqatil, Qatada, and al-Suddi say Moses was ignorant when he committed the deed.
rows.anchor: أي: من الجاهلين. قاله مجاهد ومقاتل وقتادة، والسدي

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says Ibn Masud's codex reads “one of the ignorant”; he treats ḍāll and jāhil as synonymous because Arabic uses both for missing a road.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: وكذا هو في حرف ابن مسعود: وأنا من الجاهلين

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The more common interpretation is that Moses had not yet received revelation from God and was ignorant at the time.
rows.anchor: كنت جاهلا لم يأتني عن الله شيء، وهذا قول أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada offers another reading of the ignorance: Moses did not know the deed would lead to a killing and did not act deliberately.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول قتادة قال: جهل نبي الله ولم يتعمد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطاء
rows.claim: In a report from Ibn Abbas through Ata, “astray” means that Moses was unaware of his Lord's prophethood.
rows.anchor: والأول معنى قول ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: {وأنا من الضالين} عن نبوة ربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says he fled from them to protect himself when he feared them.
rows.anchor: أي ذهبت (¬6) من بينكم حذرا # على نفسى.

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil says Moses fled to Midian because he feared Pharaoh's people would kill him for the man he had killed.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: {ففررت منكم} إلى مدين (¬1) لما خفتكم أن تقتلوني بمن قتلته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi interpret the wisdom God gave Moses as prophethood.
rows.anchor: يعني: نبوة. قاله ابن عباس، والسدي

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil interprets the wisdom as knowledge and understanding.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: يعني العلم والفهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the wisdom as intellect.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: عقلا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra interprets the wisdom as the Torah, but al-Wahidi rejects this as unlikely because the Torah was given after Pharaoh drowned.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: التوراة (¬5). وهو بعيد؛ لأن التوراة أوتي (¬6) بعد غرق فرعون.

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit explains the verbs as making someone a slave and cites Ruʾba's “enslavement” wording; he also says taʿabbada and aʿbada can mean taking someone as a slave.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السكيت: استعبده وعبده أي: أخذه عبدا

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾba's line uses taʿbīd for enslavement, as evidence for the wording.
rows.anchor: يرضون بالتعبيد والتأمي

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit says taʿabbadtu fulānan means I took him as a slave, just like ʿabbadtuhu, and that taʾammat means taking a woman as a bondwoman.
rows.anchor: ويقال: تعبدت فلانا، أي: اتخذته عبدا، مثل: عبدته سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further cited poetic line uses “you enslave me,” and another uses the form aʿbada for ʿabada; the poets are not named here.
rows.anchor: قول الشاعر: تعبدني نمر بن سعد .. البيت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says enslaving the Israelites means subjugating and putting them to work.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد، في قوله: {عبدت بني إسرائيل} قهرتهم واستعملتهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada paraphrases Moses as challenging Pharaoh to claim credit for making the Israelites slaves.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة في هذه الآية: يقول موسى لفرعون: أتمن علي أن اتخذت بني إسرائيل عبيدا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Moses contrasts Pharaoh's claimed favor in raising him with his enslavement of Israel, asking Pharaoh to release them with him and stop tormenting them.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: تمن علي أن ربيتني فيك وليدا (¬6)، وأنت قد استعبدت بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi reads Moses as saying Pharaoh boasts of favor while enslaving the Israelites.
rows.anchor: تمن بها علي وتستعبد بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil says Moses acknowledges Pharaoh's alleged kindness to him personally while indicting the enslavement of the Israelites.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: قال موسى: تمن علي إحسانك إلى خاصة فيما (¬2) زعمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says these collected explanations do not resolve the verse's difficulty, then frames the main disagreement as whether Moses denies any favor from Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: هذا ما ذكره المفسرون في هذه الآية. وهو لا يفتح غلقا ولا يحل مشكلا

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm says the phrase must be an incredulous question, understood as “or is that a favor?”, since Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel cannot be a favor to Moses.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب النظم: لا يحتمل قوله: {وتلك نعمة} إلا أن يكون مستفهما به

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm supports an omitted interrogative hamza with Arabic usage and a poetic example meaning “Should I rejoice?”
rows.anchor: أفرح أن أرزأ الكرام

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash similarly treats the clause as an incredulous question, with the phrase about enslaving Israel explaining or apposing to “favor.”
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ذكره هو قول الأخفش؛ قال: هذا استفهام كأنه قال: أو تلك نعمة

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Abbas rejects al-Akhfash's analysis: an interrogative cannot be omitted where it is required, especially when أم still signals a question; he cites the objectionable poetic usage “تروح من الحي أم تبتكر”.
rows.anchor: قال أبو العباس: وهذا غلط لا يجوز أن يلقى الاستفهام، وهو يطلب

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq reads Moses as denying Pharaoh's alleged favor: Pharaoh enslaved Israel, seized their children, enslaved or killed whom he wished, and thereby caused Moses to be brought to Pharaoh's house.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن إسحاق بن يسار في هذه الآية: أقبل موسى على فرعون ينكر عليه ما ذكر من يده عنده

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj prefers the denial reading: “What favor was enslaving Israel to me?” The declarative wording rebukes Pharaoh, since his killing of Israelite sons forced Moses' mother to put him in the river.
rows.anchor: واختار الزجاج والأزهري هذا القول وشرحاه؛ قال الزجاج: المفسرون أخرجوا هذا على جهة الإنكار

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari explains that if Pharaoh had not enslaved Israel, Moses' family would have raised him rather than casting him into the river; the supposed favor arose from Pharaoh's forbidden oppression.
rows.anchor: وزاد الأزهري بيانا لهذا القول؛ فقال: إن فرعون لما قال لموسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument works like telling someone who boasts of raising you that he could do so only after killing your parents: naming the cause rebuts the claimed favor.
rows.anchor: ونظير هذا من الكلام أن يمنن إنسان على غيره تربيته فيقول له المخاطب

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad likewise says Pharaoh raised Moses because of his oppression and attempted domination of Moses' people; grammatically, “that” begins the sentence, “a favor you claim” is its predicate, and “enslaving” explains the favor.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا القول أشار (¬5) المبرد؛ فقال: التربية كانت بالسبب الذي ذكره الله من التعبيد

rows.speaker: الفراء، وأبو العباس
rows.claim: Al-Farra and Abu al-Abbas accept that Moses acknowledges Pharaoh's upbringing as a favor: he raised Moses and spared him from the enslavement imposed on Israel.
rows.anchor: القول الثاني: أن موسى أقر بنعمة التربية. وهو قول الفراء (¬1)، ومذهب أبي العباس (¬2)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra's reading supplies an understood “and left me”: just as a spared servant may call it a favor that another was beaten, Moses contrasts his upbringing with Israel's enslavement.
rows.anchor: ومثله في الكلام: أن تضرب أحد عبيدك وتترك الآخر، فيقول المتروك: هذه نعمة علي

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra allows أن to be nominative as apposition or accusative after an understood preposition, respectively yielding “your enslaving Israel” or “because you enslaved Israel.”
rows.anchor: وقد تكون {أن} رفعا ونصبا، أما الرفع فعلى قولك: وتلك نعمة تمنها علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi explains that the acceptance reading can be reconstructed with an omitted phrase: “the favor you mention, which you claim because you enslaved Israel.”
rows.anchor: كأنه قال: وتلك التي (¬4) تذكر نعمة لك تمنها علي لأن عبدت بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says the commentators' explanations show that the denial of Pharaoh's favor is the preferred interpretation.
rows.anchor: ومذهب المفسرين: الإنكار. وما حكينا من أقوالهم يدل على الإنكار

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Pharaoh asks Moses to describe the deity who sent him, effectively asking, “What is this god of yours?”
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن إسحاق: يستوصفه إلهه الذي أرسله إليه. أي: ما إلهك هذا؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers by pointing to God's created signs, whose likeness creatures cannot produce.
rows.anchor: فأجابه موسى بما هو دليل على الله -عز وجل- مما خلق مما يعجز المخلوقين

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari asks how Moses' answer fits Pharaoh's question: “what” normally asks for a kind or lineage, answered either with a known specific identity or with a genus such as human, animal, or wall.
rows.anchor: قال ابن (¬3) الأنباري: يقال: كيف استجاز موسى حين سأله فرعون أن يجيبه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: One answer is that Pharaoh's question is misconceived because God has no genus; Moses therefore bypasses it and describes God's power, dominion, and authority to rebuke Pharaoh's ignorance.
rows.anchor: والجواب أن فرعون أحال في سؤاله، فسأل عن جنس من لا جنس له

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: A second answer is that Moses understood Pharaoh to seek knowledge of the one in question, so he answered with attributes he knew of God rather than the question's literal form.
rows.anchor: والجواب الثاني: أن موسى علم أن قصده في السؤال معرفة من سأل عنه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: A third possibility is that Moses knew Pharaoh already knew God was Lord but pretended otherwise, and understood the question as asking about God's dominion; Arabic permits an answer naming the regions ruled.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن موسى علم أن فرعون يعلم أن الله ربه؛ وإن أظهر غير ما يعلم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi interprets “if you are certain” as meaning that God created all that.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: {إن كنتم موقنين} أنه خلق ذلك

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The people of meaning say “if you are certain” means that you affirm what you directly perceive; whoever confirms sensible and rational truths should recognize the Creator when seeing created things.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: {إن كنتم موقنين} أن ما تعاينونه كما تعاينونه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says Pharaoh was confounded by Moses' answer and had no reply that could overturn it, so he appealed to those around him.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: لما قال موسى: {رب السماوات والأرض وما بينهما} تحير فرعون ولم يرد جوابا ينقض به هذا القول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the appeal as “will you not listen to what Moses says?”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد ألا تستمعون مقالة موسى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says the courtiers do not answer because Moses is addressing Pharaoh; Moses identifies the one he calls them to worship as the Lord of Pharaoh and his earliest ancestors.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: إنما لم يجبه الملأ، لأن موسى كان المراد بالجواب

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq explains that God created the earlier ancestors and created Pharaoh's generation from them.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن إسحاق: الذي خلق آباءكم الأولين، وخلقكم من آبائكم

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq explains Pharaoh's accusation as saying Moses' speech is unsound because Moses claims to have a god other than Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن إسحاق أي: ما هذا بكلام صحيح إذ يزعم أن له إلها غيري

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The people of meaning say both Pharaoh's appeal to listen and his charge of madness show inability to answer the proof; Moses ignores the insult and adds another proof.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: كلا المقالتين من فرعون مقالة العاجز عن الاعتراض على الحجة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil interprets “if you understand” as understanding God's oneness.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: إن كنتم تعقلون توحيد الله

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The people of meaning say that rational people would not miss Moses' point, as in the earlier challenge to be certain.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: إن كنتم ذوي عقول لم يخف عليكم ما أقول

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says Pharaoh did not offer a counterargument to any of these proofs.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: فلم يجبه في هذه الأشياء بنقيض لحجته

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil says the idols were made from gold, silver, iron, copper, and wood.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: وكانت أصناما من ذهب وفضة وحديد ونحاس وخشب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Maqatil gloss remaining devoted to them as staying to worship the idols and continuing without turning away.
rows.anchor: فنقيم عليها عابدين مقيمين على عبادتها لا نعدل بها شيئا. قاله ابن عباس ومقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earliest ancestors are the people of the distant past.
rows.anchor: يعني الماضين الأولين

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi takes “they are enemies to me” as Abraham's disavowal of the idols; Maqatil paraphrases it as “I am free of them.”
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: يقول أبرأ منهم

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil glosses the statement as “I am disavowed from them.”
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: أنا بريء منهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains their enmity as the idols becoming opposition and enemies to their worshippers until the Resurrection, linking this to their future disavowal of worship.
rows.anchor: ومعنى عداوة الأصنام له هو ما ذكره الفراء، أي: لو عبدتهم كانوا إلى يوم القيامة ضدا وعدوا

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutaybah calls the wording an inversion meaning “I am their enemy,” since whoever is opposed also opposes the one who opposes him.
rows.anchor: وذكر ابن قتيبة هذه الآية في باب المقلوب؛ وقال: المعنى: فإني عدو لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says later writers attribute the inverted reading to al-Farra, but he has not found that attribution in al-Farra.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا حكى بعض المتأخرين عن الفراء، ولم أر له ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular noun ʿaduww may apply to a group because it is used in place of a verbal noun, so it does not take dual or plural endings; when a verbal noun is used as an adjective-as-noun, it may be inflected.
rows.anchor: والعدو: اسم يجوز إطلاقه على الجماعة، كما قال: {وهم لكم عدو}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says “except the Lord of the worlds” can be an exception outside the preceding group: Abraham worships God and does not disavow Him; alternatively, he disavows everything they worship apart from God, since they equated their idols with Him.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: قال النحويون: إنه استثناء ليس من الأول

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil says they knew God was their Lord and Creator, and acknowledging Him as Creator counted as worship.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ذكره هو مذهب مقاتل في هذه الآية؛ قال: إنهم كانوا يعلمون أن الله ربهم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi interprets the exception as meaning “unless there is among you someone who worships God.”
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: {إلا رب العالمين} يقول: إلا أن يكون فيكم أحد يعبد # الله

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl prefers the interpretation “except whoever worships the Lord of the worlds,” which requires an omitted noun for “worshipper” and is also an exception outside the first group.
rows.anchor: واختار الحسين بن الفضل هذا القول، وقال: يعني إلا من عبد رب العالمين

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm prefers inversion because idols cannot hate anyone: “they are my enemies” means “I am their enemy”; enmity means hatred, disavowal, and refusal to agree, and its root conveys passing beyond or leaving behind.
rows.anchor: واختار صاحب النظم في قوله: {فإنهم عدو لي} القلب؛ وقال: لأن الأصنام لا تعادي أحدا

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: For “except the Lord of the worlds,” al-Naẓm's author proposes fronting and delay and takes illā as “apart from/besides,” so the exception qualifies the idols mentioned first.
rows.anchor: وقال في قوله: {إلا رب العالمين} إنه على التقديم والتأخي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi rejects that rearranged construction as strained; he also answers the objection to an exception outside the first group: a prophet knows his standing with God, and prophethood entails that God is his ally.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ذكره فيه تعد واستكراه، ثم استبعد قول الذين قالوا: إنه استثناء ليس من الأول

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses “He guides me” as “He directs me.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يرشدني

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says God guides Abraham to religion.
rows.anchor: وقال # الكلبي: فهو يهدين إلى الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone guides to religion and right direction, not the idols, because Abraham's opponents claimed their gods guided them; the creator is the guide.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: فهو الذي يهدين إلى الدين، والرشد، لا ما تعبدون من الأصنام

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm says the fāʾ, rather than wāw, connects the guidance clause as a response or consequence of the preceding creation clause.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب النظم: وجاءت الفاء دون الواو في (فهو) لأن الفاء تجعل ما بعدها متصلا بما قبلها

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm says the emphatic pronoun huwa indicates that no one besides God feeds and gives drink.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب النظم: صحول {هو} دليل على أنه أعلم أنه لا يطعم ولا يسقي غيره

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Naẓm says the fāʾ again links illness and healing as it linked creation and guidance: against claims that sickness comes from people, time, or food and healing from doctors or medicines, Abraham says God is the one who causes illness and heals.
rows.anchor: قال: دخلت الفاء هاهنا كما دخلت في الخلق والهداية، وذلك أنهم كانوا يقولون: المرض منا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi objects that this reading would require “when He makes me ill”; the verse instead says “when I become ill,” following ordinary speech that does not explicitly attribute the illness to God, even though illness is created by God's decree.
rows.anchor: وكان يجب على ما قال أن يكون: وإذا أمرضني، وقد قال: {وإذا مرضت}

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil glosses the expression “and the one who causes me to die” with “I hope,” completing the sense of Abraham's hope in the following clause.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {والذي يميتني} قال مقاتل: أرجو

rows.speaker: مجاهد، ومقاتل، والكلبي، والحسن
rows.claim: Mujahid, Maqatil, al-Kalbi, and Hasan identify the sin as Abraham's statements to Sarah that she was his sister, that he was sick, and that the largest idol had done it—the three lies.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد، ومقاتل، والكلبي، والحسن (¬5)، هي قوله لسارة: أختي، وقوله: {إني سقيم}

rows.speaker: الكلبي والحسن
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and Hasan add Abraham's statement about the stars, “This is my Lord,” to the reported sins.
rows.anchor: وزاد الكلبي والحسن قوله للكواكب: {هذا ربي}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says prophets are human and may commit sin, but not major sins, because they are protected from them.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: معنى {خطيئتي} أن الأنبياء بشر، وقد يجوز أن تقع عليهم الخطيئة

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The people of meaning say Abraham's use of “I hope” is a tactful, humble way of asking God for forgiveness.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني في قوله: (أطمع) هذا تلطف من إبراهيم في حسن الاستدعاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Day of Judgment is the Day of recompense.
rows.anchor: قوله: {يوم الدين} يريد يوم الجزاء. قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Maqatil says the Day of Judgment is the Day of accounting.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: يعني يوم الحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of “benefit” is omitted because it is understood: wealth and children will benefit no one.
rows.anchor: ومفعول النفع محذوف للعلم به كأنه قيل: لا ينفع مال ولا بنون أحدا
